div.question: What is divergence?
div.hint: Consider the flux through the faces of a tiny closed box.
div.solution: Divergence is the net outward flux per unit volume in the limit of a vanishing volume: $\nabla\cdot\vec V$.

pos.question: Define the position (radius) vector.
pos.solution: It is the directed displacement from the chosen origin O to the point P, $\vec r=\overrightarrow{OP}$.

unit.question: Define a unit vector.
unit.hint: Think about direction separately from length.
unit.solution: A unit vector has magnitude one. Along a nonzero vector A it is $\vec A/|\vec A|$.

zero.question: What is a null vector?
zero.hint: Imagine coincident start and end points.
zero.solution: Its magnitude is zero and it has no uniquely defined direction.

curl.question: Define curl.
curl.hint: Imagine a tiny paddle wheel in the field.
curl.solution: Curl, $\nabla\times\vec V$, measures local circulation per unit area. Its direction is the local axis of rotation given by the right-hand rule.

lap.question: What is Laplace’s equation?
lap.hint: Recall the sum of second spatial derivatives.
lap.solution: In a source-free region the scalar potential satisfies $\nabla^2\phi=0$.

line.question: Define collinear vectors.
line.hint: Compare lines of action, not lengths.
line.solution: They lie along the same line or parallel lines; their senses may agree or oppose each other.

plane.question: Define coplanar vectors.
plane.hint: Think of translating free arrows to a common origin.
plane.solution: Their directions can all lie in one plane; the scalar triple product of any three is zero.

bound.question: Define a localized vector.
bound.hint: Can you move its tail freely?
bound.solution: Its point of application is specified; moving it can change its physical meaning.

axes.question: What are Cartesian unit vectors?
axes.hint: Look along the positive coordinate axes.
axes.solution: They are three mutually perpendicular vectors of unit magnitude pointing along positive x, y and z.

op.question: What is a vector differential operator?
op.hint: Pair each partial derivative with its coordinate direction.
op.solution: The del operator is $\nabla=\hat i\partial_x+\hat j\partial_y+\hat k\partial_z$. It acts on fields rather than representing a displacement.

abs.question: What is absolute humidity?
abs.hint: Identify the mass in a sample of moist air.
abs.solution: Absolute humidity is the mass of water vapour per unit volume of air.

elastic.question: Define an elastic collision.
elastic.solution: Total momentum and total kinetic energy of the isolated system are both conserved.

period.question: Define temporal periodicity.
period.hint: Follow the state at one fixed position.
period.solution: A quantity is periodic in time if it repeats after a fixed interval T: $f(t+T)=f(t)$.

spin.question: What is angular momentum?
spin.hint: Measure position from the point about which rotation is considered.
spin.solution: Angular momentum is the moment of linear momentum, $\vec L=\vec r\times\vec p$.

dew.question: What is the dew point?
dew.hint: Cool an air sample without changing its vapour content.
dew.solution: It is the temperature at which the air becomes saturated and condensation can begin.

scalar.question: What is a scalar field?
scalar.hint: What information is needed at each position?
scalar.solution: A scalar field assigns a single scalar value to each point, as in a temperature distribution.

recip.question: What is a reciprocal vector?
recip.hint: Compare direction and the product of magnitudes.
recip.solution: For a nonzero vector A its reciprocal has the same direction and reciprocal magnitude: $\vec A/|\vec A|^2$.

tri.question: State the triangle law of vector addition.
tri.hint: Arrange two arrows head to tail.
tri.solution: If two sides taken in order represent the addends, the arrow from the first tail to the last head represents their sum.

grad.question: Define the gradient of a scalar field.
grad.hint: Compare rates of change in different directions.
grad.solution: Its components are the three spatial partial derivatives. It points in the direction of steepest increase; its magnitude is that maximum rate.

equal.question: What are equal vectors?
equal.hint: Check direction as well as length.
equal.solution: Vectors of the same kind are equal when their magnitudes and directions agree.

cg.question: What is the centre of gravity?
cg.hint: Replace distributed weights by one resultant.
cg.solution: It is the point through which the resultant weight acts.

spring.question: What is a spring constant?
spring.solution: Within the linear elastic range, $F=-kx$; k is the restoring force magnitude per unit extension.

surface.question: What is an area vector?
surface.hint: A plane admits a normal direction.
surface.solution: Its magnitude is the surface area and its direction is the chosen unit normal.

axiom.question: What is a postulate?
axiom.hint: Distinguish an assumption from a deduction.
axiom.solution: It is a starting proposition accepted without proof within a theory.

flow.question: What is turbulent flow?
flow.solution: Velocity fluctuates irregularly in space and time, with eddies and mixing rather than smooth layers.

humidity.question: Define relative humidity.
humidity.hint: Compare actual vapour pressure with saturation at the same temperature.
humidity.solution: It is the actual water-vapour pressure divided by the saturation vapour pressure at that temperature, expressed as a percentage.

cross.question: Define vector multiplication (the cross product).
cross.solution: $\vec A\times\vec B$ has magnitude $AB\sin\theta$ and points normal to the two vectors by the right-hand rule.

torque.question: Define torque.
torque.hint: What distance matters about a pivot?
torque.solution: Torque is the moment of force about a point: $\vec\tau=\vec r\times\vec F$.

hand.question: State the right-hand screw rule.
hand.solution: Turn it from the first vector towards the second through the smaller angle. Its advance gives the direction of their cross product.

pitch.question: What is pitch?
pitch.hint: Follow one complete turn of a screw.
pitch.solution: Pitch is the axial advance of the screw in one complete revolution.

disp.question: Define displacement vector.
disp.hint: Compare endpoints rather than the route between them.
disp.solution: It is final position minus initial position: $\Delta\vec r=\vec r_f-\vec r_i$.

weight.question: What is weightlessness?
weight.hint: Consider the reading on a weighing scale.
weight.solution: It is zero apparent weight: there is no supporting reaction, even though gravity may still act.

polar.question: What is a polar vector?
polar.solution: A polar vector transforms like displacement, reversing under inversion. Force and velocity are examples.

epoch.question: What is epoch in simple harmonic motion?
epoch.hint: Write the phase as a function of time.
epoch.solution: It is the initial phase, the phase angle at time zero.

dof.question: Define degrees of freedom.
dof.solution: The number of independent coordinates required to specify a system’s configuration is its number of degrees of freedom.

osc.question: What is oscillatory motion?
osc.hint: Watch the motion relative to equilibrium.
osc.solution: It is repeated to-and-fro motion about an equilibrium position.

unlike.question: Define unlike vectors.
unlike.hint: Compare the senses of parallel arrows.
unlike.solution: They are vectors of the same kind directed in opposite senses along parallel lines.

ineffective.question: What is an ineffective vector?
ineffective.hint: Consider a displacement that returns to its starting point.
ineffective.solution: Here the term denotes the null vector: its magnitude is zero, so adding it has no effect on another vector.

proj.question: Define scalar projection.
proj.hint: Drop a perpendicular onto the reference line.
proj.solution: The signed component of A along B is $\vec A\cdot\vec B/|\vec B|=A\cos\theta$.

quantity.question: What is a physical quantity?
quantity.hint: How would you report a measurement?
quantity.solution: It is a measurable property expressed by a numerical value and a unit.

vectorfield.question: Define a vector field.
vectorfield.hint: What must be given at each point?
vectorfield.solution: It assigns a vector, with magnitude and direction, to each point of a region.

law.question: What is a physical law?
law.hint: Distinguish a repeatable relationship from one observation.
law.solution: A law expresses a consistent relationship between physical quantities under specified conditions.

base.question: What is a fundamental unit?
base.hint: Is the unit derived from other units in the system?
base.solution: It is an independently chosen unit for a base quantity, such as the metre for length.

sand.question: Why is walking on sand difficult?
sand.solution: The foot pushes backwards. Loose sand gives way, reducing the forward frictional reaction and making each step less effective.

windshield.question: Why does vertical rain wet the front of a moving vehicle rather than its rear vertical window?
windshield.solution: In the vehicle frame the drops have a backward horizontal component as well as a downward one. They approach the front; the rear is sheltered in this geometry.

divscalar.question: Why is divergence a scalar?
divscalar.hint: Look at how del combines with the field.
divscalar.solution: The dot product adds the three component derivatives into one signed number. It gives net outward flow, not a direction.

jsign.question: Explain why $\hat k\times\hat j$ is a unit vector.
jsign.hint: Consider the order of the axes.
jsign.solution: The factors are perpendicular unit vectors, so the magnitude is one; reversing cyclic order gives $-\hat i$.

trolley.question: Why is a trolley handle long?
trolley.hint: At a fixed hand height compare the angle to the ground.
trolley.solution: A longer handle can make a smaller angle to the horizontal. The same pull then has a greater forward component $F\cos\theta$.

flux.question: Explain the physical significance of divergence.
flux.hint: Compare flow into and out of a small volume.
flux.solution: For a velocity field positive divergence indicates net local outflow, negative divergence net inflow, and zero divergence no net volume flux per unit volume.

fixed.question: Why is a position vector localized?
fixed.hint: Change the tail without changing the arrow.
fixed.solution: It begins at a specified origin. Moving its tail would no longer locate the same point relative to that origin.

bucket.question: Why can water stay in a bucket swinging in a vertical circle?
bucket.hint: Consider the top of the path.
bucket.solution: There the required acceleration is downward. Gravity and any bucket force supply it; with sufficient speed, $v^2/r\ge g$, the water maintains contact.

bisect.question: Why does the resultant of two equal vectors bisect their angle?
bisect.hint: Draw the parallelogram and its diagonal.
bisect.solution: The parallelogram is a rhombus. Its diagonal separates two congruent triangles, so the angles between the resultant and the two addends are equal.

sumdiff.question: Can two vectors have equal sum and difference?
sumdiff.hint: Distinguish vector equality from equal magnitudes.
sumdiff.solution: Vector equality A+B=A−B requires B=0. Equal magnitudes instead require A·B=0, as follows by squaring both magnitudes.

idot.question: Why is $\hat i\cdot\hat i$ not zero?
idot.hint: What is the angle of a vector with itself?
idot.solution: Both lengths are one and the angle is zero, so the dot product is one.

centrip.question: On what does centripetal force depend?
centrip.hint: Relate inward acceleration to the radius.
centrip.solution: Its magnitude is $mv^2/r$: proportional to mass and speed squared, inversely proportional to radius.

closed.question: When is the resultant of three vectors zero?
closed.solution: They sum to zero when placed head to tail in a closed triangle, so the final head returns to the starting point.

ijk.question: Show that $\hat i\times\hat j=\hat k$.
ijk.hint: Use the right hand in a right-handed coordinate system.
ijk.solution: The magnitude is sin 90° = 1; curling from positive x towards positive y makes the thumb point along positive z.

commute.question: Explain why the parallelogram law obeys commutation.
commute.solution: The same diagonal joins the common tail to the opposite corner in either order: A+B=B+A.

anti.question: Does vector multiplication commute? Explain.
anti.hint: Reverse the order of the two arrows.
anti.solution: The magnitude remains AB sin θ but the right-hand direction reverses. Thus A×B=−B×A, unequal unless the product is zero.

work.question: Why is work scalar although force and displacement are vectors?
work.hint: Consider the component of force parallel to displacement.
work.solution: Work is their dot product $Fs\cos\theta$. It is signed but has no spatial direction.

roller.question: Why is pulling a lawn roller easier than pushing it?
roller.hint: Compare the vertical components of the applied forces.
roller.solution: An upward pull reduces the normal reaction; a downward push increases it. With resistance increasing with the load, pushing is harder.

zerowork.question: When can work be zero?
zerowork.hint: Examine the factors in the scalar product.
zerowork.solution: For constant force, W=Fs cos θ vanishes for zero force, zero displacement or mutually perpendicular force and displacement.

door.question: Why is a door handle near its outer edge?
door.solution: For the same force the torque increases with perpendicular distance from the hinge, so less force is needed farther out.

rightcross.question: How should a boat be steered to land directly opposite?
rightcross.hint: Consider the component parallel to the banks.
rightcross.solution: Aim upstream so that the upstream component of the boat’s velocity relative to water cancels the current.

recipline.question: Is a reciprocal vector collinear with its original?
recipline.solution: Yes. The reciprocal is a positive scalar multiple of the nonzero original, so their lines are parallel.

worktorque.question: Compare the units and physical meanings of work and torque.
worktorque.hint: Compare a dot product with a cross product.
worktorque.solution: Both have dimensions force times length. Work is a scalar in joules; torque is an axial vector in newton metres.

fieldgrad.question: Can a vector differential operator turn a scalar into a vector?
fieldgrad.solution: Yes. The gradient of a scalar field combines its partial derivatives along each axis into a vector pointing towards the steepest increase.

perpdot.question: Can two nonzero vectors have zero dot product?
perpdot.solution: Yes: for perpendicular nonzero vectors, cos 90° = 0.

centraltime.question: Can an object moving at constant speed around a circle accelerate?
centraltime.solution: Yes. Even at fixed speed the direction changes continuously, giving inward acceleration $v^2/r$.

conserve.question: In what sense is a conservative force path independent?
conserve.hint: Compare two paths between the same endpoints.
conserve.solution: It is the work of the force that is path independent: W=U(initial)−U(final). Its integral around a closed path is zero.

unequal.question: Can two unequal vectors of the same kind have zero resultant?
unequal.solution: No. Complete cancellation requires equal magnitudes and opposite directions.

fan.question: Why does a rotating ceiling fan move air downward?
fan.hint: Distinguish blade velocity from the force on the air.
fan.solution: Pitched blades deflect air and create a pressure difference. The downward airflow is not the tangential velocity of a blade tip.

fixed18.question: Explain why $\vec r=5\hat i+3\hat j$ is a localized position vector.
fixed18.hint: Distinguish a position from a free displacement.
fixed18.solution: Its tail is at the chosen origin and its head is at (5,3). Moving its tail would no longer specify that position.

jcross.question: Explain why $\hat j\times\hat k$ is a unit vector.
jcross.hint: Consider the angle between the axes.
jcross.solution: The magnitude is 1×1×sin90°=1 and the cyclic order gives the +x direction.

dotcross.question: Can the magnitude of A×B equal A·B?
dotcross.solution: Yes. For nonzero vectors making 45°, AB sin45° and AB cos45° are equal.

vecscalar.question: How can a vector quantity be converted to a scalar?
vecscalar.hint: Think of measuring its component along a reference direction.
vecscalar.solution: Dotting it with a unit vector gives a signed scalar projection. For a vector field its divergence is also a scalar field.

volumechange.question: Does divergence help determine a change in a fluid element’s volume?
volumechange.solution: For a small material element of volume V, the fractional rate of expansion is (1/V)dV/dt=div u, where u is the velocity field.

rollerpush.question: Why does a lawn roller feel heavier when pushed?
rollerpush.hint: Draw the vertical component of the push.
rollerpush.solution: A sloping push adds a downward component, increasing the normal reaction and rolling resistance without changing the roller’s actual weight.

potential.question: What does a gravitational potential of 12 J/kg mean?
potential.hint: Consider energy per unit test mass.
potential.solution: Relative to the chosen reference, each kilogram at the point has 12 J of gravitational potential energy. The numerical sign depends on the reference convention.

negvsrecip.question: Explain why the angle between the negative and reciprocal of a nonzero vector is fixed.
negvsrecip.hint: Draw both relative to the original arrow.
negvsrecip.solution: The negative points opposite the original; the reciprocal points along it. The angle between them is always 180°.

nulldir.question: Does a zero vector have a definite direction?
nulldir.hint: Imagine its tail and head coinciding.
nulldir.solution: No. Its projection is zero on every axis and it cannot be normalized to a direction vector.

inertia.question: Distinguish mass from moment of inertia.
inertia.hint: Which quantity depends on the rotation axis?
inertia.solution: Mass measures inertia in translation. Moment of inertia measures rotational inertia and depends on how mass is distributed relative to the axis: $I=\sum mr^2$.

pole.question: Why does a tightrope walker carry a pole?
pole.hint: Consider the response to a disturbing torque.
pole.solution: The pole spreads mass farther from the rotation axis and increases the moment of inertia. A given torque then produces less angular acceleration, allowing more time to correct the tilt.

terminal.question: Why can a sphere falling through liquid acquire constant speed?
terminal.solution: As speed increases drag rises. When buoyancy plus drag balances weight, acceleration becomes zero and the sphere continues at terminal speed.

boats.question: How are boat and current velocities represented as vectors?
boats.hint: Name the frame for each velocity.
boats.solution: Draw the boat’s speed and heading relative to water and the water velocity relative to the bank. Their vector sum gives boat velocity relative to the bank.

vectorlaw.question: Is magnitude plus direction sufficient to make a quantity a vector?
vectorlaw.hint: Consider how two such quantities combine.
vectorlaw.solution: No. It must also transform and add according to the vector rules; finite rotations are a familiar counterexample.

cirvelocity.question: Can an object have constant velocity on a circular path?
cirvelocity.hint: Compare velocity at two different points.
cirvelocity.solution: No. Speed may be constant, but the tangent direction continually changes, so the velocity changes.

friction.question: Which is larger: limiting static or kinetic friction?
friction.hint: Compare the force immediately before sliding with that during sliding.
friction.solution: For typical dry surfaces the limiting static coefficient exceeds the kinetic coefficient. At the same normal load the limiting friction is larger.

orbit.question: Compare the speeds of satellites of different masses in the same circular orbit.
orbit.solution: $GMm/r^2=mv^2/r$ gives $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$. At the same orbital radius the speeds are equal, independent of satellite mass.

centralwork.question: Why does a centripetal force do no work?
centralwork.hint: Draw the instantaneous displacement tangent to the circle.
centralwork.solution: The force is radial and perpendicular to the displacement, so its dot product with the displacement is zero.

momentumreading.question: What does an angular momentum of 2400 kg m²/s mean?
momentumreading.hint: Relate angular momentum to moment of inertia and angular speed.
momentumreading.solution: About the stated axis the rotational momentum has magnitude 2400 kg m²/s; for fixed-axis rigid rotation Iω=2400. This does not by itself determine torque.

gas.question: At equal temperature do different one-mole ideal gas samples have the same mean translational kinetic energy?
gas.solution: Yes. Each molecule has mean translational energy 3kT/2; one mole has 3RT/2, independent of molecular species.

shm.question: Describe the acceleration–displacement graph for simple harmonic motion.
shm.solution: $a=-\omega^2x$: the graph is a straight line through the origin with slope −ω². Acceleration always points towards equilibrium.

jicross.question: Why is $\hat j\times\hat i=-\hat k$?
jicross.hint: Reverse the order of the usual cyclic product.
jicross.solution: Interchanging two factors reverses the cross product. Since i×j=k, j×i=−k.

birdturn.question: How can a bird change direction in flight?
birdturn.hint: Consider the direction of the resultant aerodynamic force.
birdturn.solution: By tilting its wings or using unequal wing forces, it creates a lateral component of the aerodynamic force. That acceleration changes the direction of flight.

bird.question: Explain bird flight using vector addition.
bird.hint: Resolve aerodynamic forces parallel and perpendicular to the ground.
bird.solution: The forces from the wings add vectorially. Their upward resultant component can balance weight, while a forward component supplies thrust against drag.

rope.question: Why use a long rope to tow a boat from the bank?
rope.hint: Compare the rope angle at a fixed lateral separation.
rope.solution: A longer rope can make a smaller angle to the desired direction. More of the tension then acts along the river rather than pulling towards the bank.

blades.question: If rotating fan blades suddenly shorten, what happens to the rpm?
blades.hint: Consider angular momentum during the short change.
blades.solution: If mass moves inward and external torque is negligible, the moment of inertia falls. With Iω conserved the angular speed and rpm rise.

rh.question: What does 50% relative humidity mean?
rh.hint: Compare actual and saturation vapour pressures at the same temperature.
rh.solution: The actual water-vapour pressure is half the saturation pressure at the air temperature.

lineequal.question: Why are not all collinear vectors equal?
lineequal.solution: Collinear vectors may differ in length or point in opposite directions. Equality requires both magnitude and direction to agree.

banked.question: Why is the outer edge of a curved road raised?
banked.hint: Resolve the normal reaction on the vehicle.
banked.solution: Banking gives the normal reaction an inward horizontal component that supplies part or all of the centripetal force, reducing reliance on friction.

butterfly.question: Which coordinate system can describe a butterfly moving around your room?
butterfly.hint: Count the independent directions of motion.
butterfly.solution: Use three Cartesian coordinates relative to a fixed corner or other origin. Two coordinates cannot describe changes in height as well as horizontal motion.

fanspeed.question: Why do all points on a rigid fan have the same angular velocity about its axis?
fanspeed.solution: In a given time every point turns through the same angle as the rigid fan. Angular speed is therefore common although tangential speed ωr varies with radius.

gravitywork.question: Explain why gravity is a conservative force.
gravitywork.hint: Compare the work along two routes joining the same heights.
gravitywork.solution: The work equals the loss of gravitational potential energy and depends only on the endpoints. Around a closed path the net work by gravity is zero.
